deep.reconstruction:
Problem: an entire function f(z)=Σ c_n z^n satisfies |c_n| ≤ (coefficients of) h(z), where h is entire of genus 0. Suppose also that the nonzero zeros z_i of f satisfy Σ 1/|z_i| < ∞. Claim: f has genus 0, i.e. f(z)=e^{α} z^m ∏(1 - z/z_i), with no factor e^{βz}.

Step 1 (reduction of the majorant). Write h = c z^p ∏(1 - z/a_j) with Σ1/|a_j| < ∞. Its coefficients are dominated in modulus by those of k∏(1+α_j z) with α_j = 1/|a_j| ≥ 0 and Σα_j < ∞; the power z^p can be absorbed. So one may take h = k∏(1+α_i z).

Step 2 (growth of f). |f(z)| ≤ Σ|c_n||z|^n ≤ h(|z|). For such a product, log h(r) = Σ log(1+α_i r) = o(r). Hence |h(z)| ≤ C_ε e^{ε|z|} for every ε > 0. So f has order ≤ 1, and in fact minimal exponential type (exponential type 0).

Step 3 (Hadamard factorization). By Hadamard and the summability of the zeros, f = e^{α+βz} z^m ∏(1 - z/z_i). It remains to show β = 0.

Step 4 (normalising β). If β ≠ 0, replace f(z) by f(θz) with θ = β̄/|β|. This does not change |c_n|, so the majorization by h is preserved, and the exponential becomes e^{|β|z}. One may therefore assume β > 0. Then |f(z)| = K e^{βx} |z|^m ∏|1 - z/z_i|.

Step 5 (sector estimate). The crossed-out lines are a first attempt at the next step; the next page completes it. In a sector |arg z| ≤ θ one has x ≥ c|z| with c > 0. Combined with |f| ≤ C_ε e^{ε|z|} and ε < c, the canonical part g(z)=z^m∏(1 - z/z_i) satisfies |g(z)| ≤ k e^{-a|z|} in that sector. Since g itself has genus 0, |g(z)| ≤ k' e^{(a/3)|z|} everywhere.

Step 6 (rotation trick). Put G(z)=g(z)g(ωz)g(ω²z) with ω = e^{2πi/3}. For every z, at least one of z, ωz, ω²z lies in the sector, provided θ ≥ π/3. Hence |G(z)| ≤ k'' e^{-(a/3)|z|}, so G is bounded and tends to 0, forcing G ≡ 0. But G(z) = z^{3m}∏(1 - z³/z_i³) is not identically zero. This contradiction gives β = 0.

Context: this is the analytic lemma behind Grothendieck's Fredholm theory (Produits tensoriels topologiques, 1955; 'La théorie de Fredholm', 1956). The Fredholm determinant det(1+zu) of a nuclear-type operator has coefficients majorized by those of ∏(1+α_i z) with Σα_i < ∞. Showing it has genus 0 when the eigenvalues are summable is exactly showing det(1+zu) = ∏(1+λ_i z), i.e. that Tr u = Σλ_i.
errors: Next page: the opening angle θ of the sector is said to be 'between π/3 and π'. To get x ≥ c|z| with c > 0 one needs θ < π/2, so the right range is π/3 ≤ θ < π/2. With θ ≥ π/2 the constant c is not positive.
The crossed-out inequality at the bottom of this page (|f(z)| ≤ |z|^m∏|1 - z/z_i| ≤ K e^{ε|z|}) is not valid as written. Grothendieck rightly abandoned it and replaced it by the sector argument.
Small gap: Step 1 (majorising a general genus-0 h, including a power z^p, by k∏(1+α_i z) with α_i ≥ 0) is asserted without proof. It is easy but not quite immediate.
The 'on vérifie aussitôt' bound for G needs the sector to cover the plane under the three rotations. This holds precisely because θ ≥ π/3, a point stated only implicitly.

ideas.what: An entire function whose coefficients are dominated by those of a genus-0 function is of minimal exponential type.
ideas.where_published: Produits tensoriels topologiques (Mem. AMS 16, 1955), Ch. II; 'La théorie de Fredholm' (Bull. SMF 1956), Fredholm determinant estimates

ideas.what: A function of order 1 and minimal type whose zeros satisfy Σ1/|z_i| < ∞ equals e^α z^m ∏(1 - z/z_i) (no e^{βz} factor).
ideas.modern_name: Lindelöf's theorem on functions of exponential type (minimal type case)
ideas.usually_credited_to: E. Lindelöf (1903); see Boas, Entire Functions, ch. 2
ideas.where_published: Used in the Fredholm determinant theory of Produits tensoriels topologiques / La théorie de Fredholm (unsure of exact formulation there)

ideas.what: Rotation trick G(z)=g(z)g(ωz)g(ω²z): exponential decay in a sector of half-opening ≥ π/3 plus minimal type everywhere forces g ≡ 0.
ideas.modern_name: Elementary substitute for Phragmén–Lindelöf / Carlson-type uniqueness

ideas.what: Genus-0 property of the Fredholm determinant ⇔ trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
ideas.modern_name: Trace formula (Grothendieck for 2/3-nuclear operators; Lidskii for trace class)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (1955/56) for 2/3-nuclear operators; V. B. Lidskii (1959) for Hilbert trace class
ideas.where_published: Produits tensoriels topologiques, Ch. II §4; La théorie de Fredholm (1956)

missed.claim: This lemma is exactly the analytic half of the now-standard proof of Lidskii's theorem (Simon, Trace Ideals). For u trace class on a Hilbert space, det(1+zu) has coefficients dominated by those of ∏(1+s_i z), where the s_i are the singular values. Weyl's inequality (1949) gives Σ|λ_i| ≤ Σ s_i < ∞, so the Proposition yields det(1+zu) = ∏(1+λ_i z) and Tr u = Σλ_i. Grothendieck had the lemma in 1953, and Weyl's inequality was available, yet the published trace formula is only stated for 2/3-nuclear operators. Lidskii's theorem came in 1959.
missed.quote: Soit f(z) une fonction entière dont les coefficients sont majorés en module par ceux d'une fonction de genre 0 h(z). Si de plus les racines non nulles z_i de f(z) sont telles que Σ 1/|z_i| < +∞, f(z) est de genre zéro.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical point for the trace-formula and eigenvalue-distribution literature (Pietsch, König, Simon). The archive shows Grothendieck held the precise abstract criterion in 1953. In Hilbert space the only missing ingredient for Lidskii was eigenvalue summability. The lemma is classical, so this is a credit and priority footnote rather than a new theorem.

deep.surprise_reason: The proposition is a classical consequence of Lindelöf's theory, and the proof is elementary, with a minor slip on the next page. Its interest lies in its abstract form: genus 0 from coefficient majorization plus summable zeros. That is precisely the criterion turning Fredholm-determinant estimates into trace = Σ eigenvalues. Combined with Weyl's inequality it would give Lidskii's theorem years early, which is a modest historical point.

'|f(z)| = K e^{βx}': in the image the constant is written as 'K^{te}' or 'C^{te}' (constante), i.e. |e^{α}|.
